utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning. Good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the registry, the OTP, the Defence counsels. I can see they're all here. Good morning to the accused. We're going to take up the testimony that we started yesterday, and we have reached the stage for the cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic. Is there a problem? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No problem, Your Honour. Good morning. The problem only lies in the fact that the rest of the Defence teams have a chance to put questions to this witness before the Prosecution goes ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, and I thank you, Mr. Krstan Simic, for bringing that to my attention. I do indeed have to ask the other Defence teams whether they have any questions to ask this witness. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence teams do not have any cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. And thank you for paying attention. Witness Samardzija, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you you're continuing your evidence under oath and will now be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution. I think it is Ms. Somers who is going to cross-examine to you. Ms. Somers, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, has any one of the other accused, either Radic, Kos, Zigic, or Prcac, been brought to your attention for any purpose the way you indicated Kvocka was brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday twice who headed the Centre for Security Services in Banja Luka where you worked. I am afraid that having reviewed the record, no name was given in response to the question. Would you please tell us what was the name of the individual who headed the Centre for Security Services in Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the head of the security services was Mr. Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin you said?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I said yesterday that Mr. Stojan Zupljanin signed the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, pleases what is the fifth sector. What does that connote?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a sector dealing with training and defence preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that is the sector in which you worked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Whom were you responsible for training?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was responsible for the training of officers, line officers at the level of the republic, as well as the head of the sector for state security.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How long were you holding the position of being responsible for training these persons, from when to when?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1986 up until the outbreak of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What date do you fix for the outbreak of the crisis?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis broke out, that is to say, there were tensions at the end of 1991 already, which was December, that is to say, when they included me in doing liaison officer work, which was the 15th of December, 1991. And quite a long time before that representatives of the European Community were in the field as monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From what point were these persons in the European Community in the field, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you specifically. But I know that according to an agreement, before I became included into these affairs, they visited Banja Luka and the surrounding areas and were put up at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, can you give us a month and a year, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1991; I think it was sometime in mid-1991. I was not involved in those activities so much before I was actually assigned the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So much, but you had some involvement with the European Community that was present at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only as of December 1991. Up until then, I had no contacts whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, some of the names of the persons with whom you dealt in the European Community?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the precise names, but there was a representative from Greece, I recall, that is to say, I could recognise him. Then there was a representative from Sweden. And I contacted directly with Major Guseinov from the Soviet Union, with Carlos from Venezuela. And then there was Abdulah Babu from -- let me just try to remember where he was from. He was from -- he was a major, I know that much. Yes, he was from Malaysia. And I think that in their reports, they noted down that they had had contacts with me. I did not make a note of the others. But I did take round representatives, I think it was, of the Red Cross. I took them to Manjaca where they looked at how the situation was there and prepared the transportation of the individuals who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me for --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. We're talking December 1991. Your contacts with the International Community representatives --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- can you tell me, please, with whom you dealt and for what purpose in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December 1991, we were given the assignment -- that is to say, several colleagues and myself were told to be liaison officers, that is to say, to ensure contacts with individuals who were representing international organisations. They had their own interpreters. I can't remember their names. But their interpreters would ask us for the people that they would like to contact, and then it was my job as the liaison officer to ensure that they had contacts with representatives of the municipality or the president of the municipality, with the religious organisations, with representatives of military units, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In fact, do you recall an order in January 1992 actually appointing you to handle these matters as liaison officer? Was there not such an order handed to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no official order. But it was probably one of the documents that were issued. I think that this was linked with contacts to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was it who put you in this liaison position? Name the official, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed by the head of the centre, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he personally tell you, or was it handed down to you by word of mouth and you just showed up one day as a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was handed down. I think that the chief of the sector told me that I had been designated for the job. But all the equipment that we had was issued by the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your work in the -- what you have described as communications and encryption, that would include, would it not, the interception of communications, wiretapping, bugging? That would be part of your function, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The nature of the CSB was essentially an intelligence service insofar as your work was concerned, was it not? The functions in which you were engaged were information gathering, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The function that I was concerned with was to train people for jobs of that kind, but there is a separate department for the kinds of activities that you have enumerated. I did not work on matters of that kind, that is to say, direct contact, but my work was to train reservists and active-duty people in these protection devices and other things concerning operative work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Protection devices. What type of protection devices?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a system used for coding, for encryption. There is a set technology. Technical -- I don't think that this is an unknown subject. You have to prepare the document on the basis of certain existing tables, and it was necessary to train people to do this in a precise manner and not to make errors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the communications aspect of what you described as your job, what did that entail?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant the use of communication devices, that is to say, to explain to people how they are used, how they are handled, and the preparations necessary for operating these devices.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What types of communications devices, telephones, telephone receiver sets? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a one-way link and a two-way link and radio receivers along that communication line, so that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You eventually became head of that department. How did your functions change insofar as training and fieldwork once you became head of that department? And when did you become head of that department, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't actually become head of that department but the next department, the other department that had concrete assignments and jobs, and that was sometime in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. Perhaps I misunderstood your testimony yesterday when Mr. Simic asked you: "Q. Did you later become head of that department?" referring to communications and encryption, and your answer was: "A. Yes." Would you like to correct that and explain?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to correct that because we -- we keep changing; that is to say, the departments changed, although they are similar within the frameworks of the department and linked to crypto-protection. But there are two lines, actually, 04 and another line that was linked firmly to crypto-protection. I continued in the crypto-protection professional section, and so being head of that section, I became head of the other one which had to do with the application of measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The type of assistance that you indicated Mr. Drljaca requested of you you called operative technical cover. "Operative" was explained as all measures at the disposal of the State Security Service. You were, in fact, an operative of that service. Can you tell us, please, your operative number?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the number just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Krstan Simic is on his feet. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I do not know the purpose of this line of questioning, whether it is to determine the structure of the state security system, or is it linked to the subject of our trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, your response, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is to explore areas that would indicate whether or not there was any substance to what was said about the requests toward Mr. Kvocka and whether or not it is a matter that -- from which any inferences on credibility can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a short reply. The witness said that Mr. Drljaca was in the police as a layman - and I explained this - and Mr. Drljaca went back to the liaison officer whom he knew was doing this kind of work in order to -- for him to be able to ensure what Mr. Drljaca has asked the witness to do, and he acted as a policeman. I don't see what there is to ascertain or what could bring into question the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But at any rate, I think that the Prosecutor is trying to explain some of the terms that were used yesterday, and if you take a look, "an operative" was, I think one of the words used yesterday, and the Prosecutor is trying to establish what is implied by that term. So I will allow the Prosecutor to continue with her questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You expressed yesterday some opinions or some impressions of yours about Simo Drljaca. I'll explore those in a moment, but I'd like to ask you, before I do that, the name of one individual. Ljuban Ecim. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who was Ljuban Ecim, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the deputy head of the centre at one period of time; otherwise, he worked in the passport department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You expressed some concern over the professionalism, as it were, of Mr. Drljaca based on his wearing Adidas sneakers when he sought you out in Banja Luka. What particular relevance could dress have on a person's professionalism?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not actually relevant. What was relevant was that the gentleman, on one occasion when I saw him in an official facility, he was wearing these white Adidas sneakers and so was not dressed in keeping with his rank, because I'd never seen the head of a police station dressed in that way before on official premises. So those were just my impressions. It was just an impression I gained, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From your testimony, it is clear that Simo Drljaca expressly and specifically sought you out. Now, this is the same Simo Drljaca who was indicted by this Tribunal for genocide and who died while resisting, with violence, the arrest for those charges. This is the same person? Are we talking about the same person?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The information that he passed on to you about suspicions of unreliability as to Serbs, you did not act on; that is correct? There was no action taken by you in instituting a wiretap or any other kind of intercept means; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you're mixing up things here. I said that I met him in a rather unusual spot, that is to say, Mr. Simo Drljaca. We happened to meet by chance; he didn't seek me out. We met by chance in the cafe, there were other people present, and that is why I said it was an unprofessional attitude, because he spoke, perhaps, under the influence of alcohol. He said what he said under the influence of alcohol, and that's why I said it was not professional. I told him to contact the chief, who would then see to the matter. He seemed to mix things up himself because I wasn't actually working on jobs of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't recall alcohol mentioned yesterday. Can you tell how you would know that he had been drinking?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is customary for everybody in a cafe to have a drink. I don't know how much he had because I joined the table of people already there. And I said what I said to, perhaps, justify his behaviour, to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Nonetheless, it appears from the numerous documents which have been admitted before this Chamber and with which they are familiar that security and loyalty and reliability were very much prerequisites for positions in the structure of that particular parastate. Can you please indicate what you did to follow up on accusations about -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My learned colleague has made a whole introduction which is leading for the question she wishes to ask, and she wishes to bring into question the affiliation of the witness to a paramilitary state, although the witness clearly said that he was a policeman from the first day and that the police continued going about its business after this portion of the Serbian -- that is to say, when Bosnia-Herzegovina came under the control of the Serbs, he continued with his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, yes, I certainly am leading; that is my right on cross-examination. Secondly, the reference was not to a paramilitary state. If it is incorrect, it should be "parastate," in my words, not "paramilitary." So if the record is incorrect -- if it is incorrect, I ask it to be corrected. And this, of course, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, it is written parastate here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I thought, parastate. And I would fully want to explore the type of allegation that was made. I think that is the guts of what was being brought in direct examination and we must certainly find out about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers. Could you put the question in a different way, without leading and without including your own judgements? So ask the question you want to ask but without including your own opinion. Whether it's a parastate or paramilitary, that's another question. Just go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For the entity in which you were working at the time, the documents as well as testimony have indicated that loyalty and reliability in Serbs was a great concern. Now, can you indicate, please, when there is a challenge, as you have said there was, to the reliability of an individual who was holding a significant police position, what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the question goes outside my own domain. Let me say again that at that time I was not working on those jobs so I can't actually tell you. All I can tell you is what I know about and what is connected to the case when Mr. Simo Drljaca requested me to do something which was not within my competency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you just to take a quick look at a document which is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It bears the Prosecution's and Registry's exhibit Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number of 2/2.7. We have copies for the Bench. If we could turn to page 2. Again, it was 2/2.7, a document dated 20 May 1992, from the Banja Luka Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask you to turn your attention to the English page 2 and paragraph 5, please. Now, this document is issued by Stojan Zupljanin, your then chief. The paragraph says: "We have to identify in time those among us who are involved in criminal activities and we must take rigorous steps against them (immediately commence disciplinary proceedings)." You did not know, did you, what the essence of the unreliability was. Did you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know what unreliability means. But for that to be proved, there must be some documentation and some facts which bear that out, which prove it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You took no measures to further find out if there were any substance to the allegations -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness answered this question twice quite definitively; that is to say, at the time when the request or proposal came to him from Mr. Drljaca, it was not within his competency, and that he then informed his seniors thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as much as I am sure that counsel wants to bring these points up, I think it is more important that the witness himself tell us what happened. In fact, there was not much exploration at all into what he did or didn't do about the allegations other than to say he passed on to a superior. The outcome of this was never explored, and I think it is absolutely essential for this Chamber to know what was done, given the background to the sanctions that could be worked upon someone who perhaps was involved in such behaviour or against whom such suspicions may have been lodged. The relevance, I think, is very, very evident. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] A brief reply, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the police force, there is a clear-cut chain of command, and in no police force in the world does the superior inform his subordinates what measures have been taken, especially when it comes to state security, where the system is a closed one and confidential and where the staff hide information from each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But there are no problems. If the Prosecutor has asked the question, the witness must answer to the best of his ability. So please go ahead with the question. The question is whether the superior informed him or not, and the witness can give a simple answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can go back, I think we may have lost our continuity. But the question is:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was any action taken? After you yourself made a decision that it was not within your competency, you passed it up to superiors. What action was taken to investigate this? What was the outcome, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that unofficially, that is to say, over a cup of coffee, I learnt that there were certain activities linked to the requests made, and they were assessed as being too broad and not technically feasible. So I think that that is a clear definition. But I was not supposed to know that officially.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who made the assessment, please? You can tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a conversation with the man who worked on those matters at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Name, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it is quite sufficient for me to say that it was a man involved in those matters, and in principle, it is a state secret. I know his name, if necessary, but I don't think it is necessary to bandy about names because it was an unofficial conversation over a cup of coffee, and the information, the comments he made, was the comment that Simo Drljaca had asked more than could be realistically accomplished with respect to the men at our disposal and the technological means, but he said that unofficially.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you were sitting and having a cup of coffee and someone said that there was an assassination attempt against Stojan Zupljanin in the works, would you act on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite normal that I would take steps to protect the head of the centre if I was able to do so at that given moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand this. It is your evidence that the only time you ever heard of Kvocka, the accused, was when you were asked, as you claim, by Drljaca to tap his conversations? That is the only time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to move on, please, to another area that you discussed, your UN and EC mission liaison work. You alluded to some of your obligations this morning. Would you tell us, please, how long did you continue to work in the capacity as liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, officially I worked as a liaison officer until April or thereabouts, but even after that, the head of the centre used my services in some situations because I knew English, so that practically I was used in such context as long as I worked there, whenever it was necessary to make a contact or to meet with international representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then can we at least establish that throughout the year 1992, you either officially by assignment or through approval of your superior or superiors were the liaison, be it officer or other title, to the UN and EC missions on behalf of your organisation? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I should add that I contacted not only with the UN but also I was in charge of contact with the Catholic church, and I had specific tasks to ensure the organisation of the visit of the Bishop to -- Mr. Franjo Komarica of Banja Luka. I had direct contacts with Mr. Franjo Komarica and his secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Two names from the international community. Could you tell me if you're familiar with them? Ian Blair, and a Mr. Barney. I don't know if it's first or last name, but Barney. Do you recall those names?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. And we find it difficult to remember foreign names. I, for instance, remembered Abdulah Babu because it's a peculiar name. I also remember the name of Mr. Guseinov because it -- I associate it with the name of the caterpillar in our language, but, otherwise, I find it difficult to remember foreign names. I have to make associations to do this, and I have to have several contacts with the person before I remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this is despite your fluency in English which is one of the bases for your being selected? You don't remember the names of Ian -- whatever names I gave you, they're not familiar?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, the witness has already answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I want to clarify some points that were a bit unclear in the transcript. You indicated that you knew Simo Drljaca, Prijedor, through the contacts that were made while you were representing -- you were acting as liaison officer to representatives of international humanitarian organisations which were going to Prijedor after dismantling of camps. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I had contacts even after that, but I knew Mr. Simo Drljaca also because I heard that he was appointed chief in Prijedor, and he would occasionally come to Banja Luka. He was a man very difficult not to remark and one could not help but remember him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The conversation that we discussed a few minutes ago, you put to a time of first few days of June or middle of June 1992, that is, the conversation between you and Mr. Drljaca, according to your evidence yesterday. Is that still accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd just like to present a document of 31 August 1992. It is Prosecution's Exhibit -- it may be 28 August 1992. It concerns the closing of the camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise to the Chamber. We thought we had everything lined up so well. It would be 28 August. It would have been 2/3.39, dated 28 August. It should be in the pile of documents which was handed to each of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are, in fact, two communications in this exhibit. The first is a confirmation signed by Simo Drljaca - since your English is okay, I trust you have no problem reading it - indicating that "there are no camps, prisons, or collection centres on the territory of the Prijedor municipality." That is August 24, 1992. The same date, the second document that is attached, the document of -- excuse me, confirming some of the facts, but if you would turn to the document signed by Stojan Zupljanin, it also refers -- and is a 24 August 1992 document. It also acknowledges certain facts about the camp. I want to make sure that you knew that as of the 28th or perhaps even the 24th of August, 1992, certain camps had been closed. That included Omarska and Keraterm. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question, considering that I had not been in Omarska or Keraterm. I think you could not draw a conclusion to the contrary from any of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: However, will you agree that the CSB in Banja Luka had responsibility for the territory on which Omarska camp and Keraterm -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My learned colleague, Your Honours, is asking for a conclusion about the responsibility of an entire body, whereas he was only an official of that body. He became head of the department only in 1995. He never was either in Omarska or Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask your question, Ms. Somers, in a way, because this witness has come to answer questions about the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the organisation for which you were working at the time had jurisdiction over the territories on which Keraterm and Omarska was located?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how it was agreed, but judging by these communications, which I have not examined, it is obvious that there was a chain of command during the war, but I cannot say anything definitively because I was not a member of that particular centre. It is clear that each SUP had responsibility towards the local community and towards their superiors on the higher level. So it's very difficult to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you did not know of the existence, during the period of operation, of Omarska and Keraterm camps?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any contacts with or access to those locations, so I cannot answer this. I cannot make any statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did any of the representatives of the International Community whom you were tasked to work with ever ask to see those camps while they were in operation, prior to the end of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that all requests addressed to me by the interpreters of international representatives, I have tried to comply with them, and they mainly had to do with the territory of Banja Luka and the territory of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: However, you said that Prijedor was on your route because you had contacts that were made while you were working with the internationals there. Did you tell them that there were camps such as Omarska and Keraterm, even if they didn't ask?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never discussed it at all, nor had anybody ever asked me this. I have already said that the most remotest point I ever visited was Trnopolje, and in the direction of Banja Luka I went as far as Manjaca. Perhaps some other liaison officer or other persons in charge of Protocol had such discussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can explain then why you accompanied these internationals to Prijedor when camps were dismantled and not when camps were operational.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me correctly. I wasn't in Prijedor. I went to Trnopolje. And I said that in the period when I had contacts with international representatives, I did not take them to Keraterm or to Trnopolje or to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you recall specifically if any of the internationals were from the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a team from the ICRC whom I took to Trnopolje and there was also another team which went to Manjaca. I think it was the International Red Cross, although, they have those difficult abbreviations, acronyms, which I find difficult to remember. There are three letters used in various combinations, and I cannot say clearly to which organisation they belonged because I wasn't particularly interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let's move on, please. The June 1992 time frame when you were discussing, when you showed -- actually, you used that time frame to refer to Trnopolje and Manjaca. The activities that were taking place in territories neighbouring Prijedor during June 1992, let us talk about them for a moment. You worked with Stojan Zupljanin. Do you know Slobodan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what, if any, relationship is he to Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they are relatives and not very close relatives at that, but I cannot be sure. I heard something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: He's his brother, is he not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say really because I don't know that. Maybe he's a cousin or a brother of his relatives, but I don't think that they're brothers, they're really brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is this the same Slobodan Zupljanin who in June 1992 was a Captain in the 22nd Light Mountain Brigade, the person you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say in which unit he served because I had no occasion to learn about that personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the 11th of June, 1992, there was a Serb takeover of power in Kotor Varos, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Kotor Varos is a municipality located 70 kilometres away from Prijedor. You arrive in Banja Luka, then you go to Celinac, which is a different municipality, and only then on to Kotor Varos. I happen to know Mr. Zupljanin, and he is from Kotor Varos, and I really see no connection between the brigade which was in Kotor Varos, deployed in Kotor Varos, and the case which has to do with Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, if the Court would permit the map to be distributed. It is in your pile of documents. It is 2/1.1. It is, of course, part of the communities that were involved in the overall Serb takeover of communities. It is under the territory of the CSB, which was the employer of this witness and, in fact, if the CSB, if the Court will permit me to continue my examination, had direct involvement in this takeover as did the witness on that day. Therefore, the witness's credibility and his activities during the time period that he has spoken about yesterday must be explored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the purpose of this line of questioning, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this individual has told us about certain activities and about his competencies during the time period relevant to this indictment and has made certain representations about his role in the CSB, which is very, very important to understanding whether or not he can be believed as to any other facts for which he was brought before the Chamber. I would like to have the opportunity to explore his role in a takeover of the municipality that occurred during the time period when he said he was otherwise engaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead. Please sit down, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This Court has heard very much testimony and has seen documentation about the takeover, the Serb takeover, of other municipalities and specifically Prijedor in 1992. Now, in a manner similar, you acknowledge that Kotor Varos was taken over on the 11th of June, 1992. Can you tell us, please, or comment: Certain non-Serbs who were arrested in Kotor Varos on that day have identified Slobodan Zupljanin as the commander of the military units which were stationed in Kotor Varos already before the takeover. Do you have any knowledge of this? Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm who was the military commander because I was a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: These non-Serbs who were arrested in Kotor Varos on the 11th have identified you, Zdravko Samardzija as the commander of the Serb units which came into Kotor Varos on the 11th of June and they described your command as over special units. Can you comment, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this statement is not accurate because I was in Kotor Varos. I was in the unit also as a liaison officer, and the chain of the command in the unit is quite clear. There is the commander, deputy commander, and I don't fit into any of those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Two of the non-Serbs that were arrested that day described you, Zdravko Samardzija, as wearing a camouflage hat and the units wearing red berets. They said that you introduced yourself as Zdravko Samardzija, a lawyer from Banja Luka. Do you have any recollection of that incident or those incidents?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, I introduced myself as Zdravko Samardzija because, pursuant to the regulations, I was doing my duty and there was no reason for me not to identify myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you inform any of the internationals from either the UN or the EC mission with whom you were working that you would be carrying out this operation, this takeover of power, on 11 June of 1992. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, the witness has said that he was liaison officer so he was involved there. What is your objection? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers is asking the question: Did you inform that you would take over power, and the witness has -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was: Did you inform the international authorities, the representatives of the International Community. That was my understanding of the question. [In English] "Did you inform any of the internationals from either the UN or the EC mission ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My associate is telling me that the English transcript says what I have just quoted, "that you would be carrying out this operation, this takeover of power." That is what I have been told. Page 24, line 10 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Mr. Krstan Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I believe that such a question cannot be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, I think that is a perfectly legitimate question to ask. This is a man in whom the trust of the International Community to represent the condition in that territory was had. I'd like to know, I think it's fair to know, whether or not -- and their safety, of course, is one of the concerns based on, I'm sure, the functions of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was: [In English] "Did you inform any of the internationals from either the UN or the EC mission with whom you were working that you would be carrying out this operation ..." [Interpretation] Witness, did you inform them or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, such notification would be contrary to our regulations and laws. Second, I learned about the operation just before it started so none of us had the opportunity to contact anyone whatsoever after receiving that order because we were immediately transferred from our current location to the location from which we would commence the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the answer is that you did not inform them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it was not my obligation to report such things because I had no such agreement with representatives of the International Community about such information being provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That would mean that if an international were to have wandered into that territory on that day and met with some type of accidental injury, that would not be your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that had happened, it would have been our responsibility. Of course we would have taken measures to prevent anything of the kind, because we took great care that nothing should happen to any member of an international organisation. On several occasions, I was in dangerous situations because certain members of international organisations could not drive in an adequate manner in areas where there was shooting. They would drive only 60 kilometres per hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That means that they would have to know there was shooting, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You evidently ask your questions in a very imprecise way. I would like you to specify with regard to what and where. You can receive an answer from me and later put it in a context which has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I thank you for your guidance. I would like to now ask you about, specifically, what laws and regulations governed the takeover of Kotor Varos, you having just mentioned that notification would have been contrary to said laws and regulations. Please be specific.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I said prior notification. At the time when a certain activity has been ordered by the head of the centre, any notification given to outsiders - I think the same applies to your bodies - unless authorised, is subject to disciplinary action and prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on. Another non-Serb victim who was detained at the sawmill following the takeover of Kotor Varos identified you, Mr. Samardzija, as being in charge of that detention facility. Did you inform the UN and the EC of your connection to that particular detention centre in the course of your dealings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not in charge of that facility. Those facilities were under the jurisdiction of the local police; the local authorities, therefore. I just interviewed certain persons in connection with the situation which we had been informed about to the effect that Muslim policemen had organised a group of 200 men, under arms, who had abandoned their jobs and left the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The non-Serb victim from Kotor Varos described your allowing men from your unit to beat him in your presence, and when on the brink of death, instructing your men not to kill him because he was needed for questioning. Can you comment, please, on this? Do you recall the incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall any such incident. There were incidents when certain members of paramilitary formations entered the area that we were in, that is, the area covered by our station, and engaged in activities that were unlawful, and I warned them every time not to do that. However, under those circumstances, we had very little chance of resisting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I think you must watch the time in view of the time allotted to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. You have preempted my next comment which is no further questions. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much. Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that my learned friend has opened a number of issues, I have only two questions linked to those that went outside the scope of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, when you said that you were a liaison officer with representatives of international organisations, at the time, were you the authority communicating and taking positions or were you a liaison officer to establish contact with them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty was to enable contact between them and our authorities so I had no right to intervene in the discussion. Very frequently, I was not even present during those conversations. For instance, when there were talks with military commanders, I usually sat outside. This also happened on a number of occasions when representatives of international organisations wanted to have a tête-à-tête with somebody. I would not attend because my job was simply to bring them safely to a place where they had an appointment with someone; to provide certain services for them; to find the people they wished to have contact with. Usually, it was with the town mayor, representatives of the religious communities, or representatives of the military commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, have I understood you correctly? In those contacts, you never represented any particular institution of the entity that was then called the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not represent any institution. I was, as the name says, a liaison officer, a man ensuring contacts and nothing more than that. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Krstan Simic. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to have certain points clarified if possible. You mentioned that you were a lawyer, you studied law. Was there any connection between your legal profession, your legal background, and the work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No. Just two minutes ago you told the Prosecutor, or in your conversation with the Prosecutor, it was mentioned that you interviewed certain persons, some 200 Muslims who abandoned their jobs and so on. Were you used sometimes -- did you take over some investigations with arrested people, for instance? Were you an investigator? Being a lawyer, was this job confined to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have occasion to engage in interviews of that kind, only rarely, however. In principle, they were just interviews for the purpose of obtaining information. I did not initiate criminal proceedings or undertake any other legal measures. I just had to collect information and pass it on to my superior. This was purely operative work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you do that in some of the concentration centres?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Where did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I engaged in such interviews with a certain number of persons in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like also to have a clarification concerning this order you got from Simo Drljaca to tap conversations. Was that a current method, as it's done sometimes, you know, in any regime, to tap conversations, or were certain people chosen because people doubted very much their loyalty? Could you tell us if this was just the current method? Although you refused it, as you said. But was this special people? You mentioned Kvocka and others. Was it a minority, limited persons, or was it a general attitude?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was limited to a few persons. Especially, as I have already said, the technical possibilities were limited, and it is very difficult to undertake such steps and it is necessary to obtain approval from a much higher level above the centre, even. So it's rather complicated to start such a procedure. It was not a customary procedure to be engaged in lightly, at someone's free will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you refuse an order with impunity and no sanction would happen against you? I mean, in the hierarchy, could anybody refuse an order?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was complicated to refuse an order because this necessarily entailed sanctions, because the standard military rule is carry out the order and complain later and the same rule applies to the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What happened to you when you refused? I hope nothing.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid you misunderstood me. Mr. Simo Drljaca was never my superior so he could not give me orders. I received orders from the head of the centre who, in the chain of command, came above Simo Drljaca, so I was protected as far as he was concerned. But I could not refuse an order from the head of the centre or from the head of the Defence Department; that would have been rather difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was only Drljaca who did not have a good opinion of Mr. Kvocka or who suspected his loyalty, but not the whole system.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what opinions people had as I personally didn't know Mr. Kvocka at all. The gist of this is that we had this conversation and that Mr. Simo Drljaca asked me to do this in the wrong place, addressing the wrong man. So all I could do was tell him how this can be done. According to my unofficial information, he tried to do something officially; but whether he succeeded or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: My last inquiry. You said that the police force had no control over the paramilitary formations. Now, these paramilitary formations were above the law, they ran wild, or were they accountable to somebody?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those formations were outside the law because these were locals who were quite aggressive, who were ready to settle accounts, even with regular police officers and members of the army. So it was very difficult to communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have just two questions, and they relate again to the conversation that you had with Mr. Drljaca in the sports club. When he said that he wanted you to investigate the unreliability of Mr. Kvocka or to investigate whether Mr. Kvocka was unreliable, you said earlier, "Well, I knew what that meant." Would you tell us what you did understand "unreliable" to mean in that context according to Mr. Drljaca. Not your own definition, necessarily, but what you understood from the conversation to be unreliable about what. Unreliable in what sense?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My perception was, at the time, that he was referring to Serbs who were collaborating with persons who had not signed loyalty to Republika Srpska or, at the time, the Republic of Krajina. So the substance of it was that that person did not fit the wishes of Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And in that conversation, did Mr. Drljaca give you any specifics? Did he mention anything? "We have reason to doubt Mr. Kvocka's unreliability use of ..." or anything, or he just said "unreliability" on that was kind of a code name for collaborationist with the enemy, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, he said that these were persons who were unreliable and who needed to be checked out. He probably had some reasons for that. I didn't inquire into the details. All I did was to say that I was not the person to do that, and I referred him to the competent body within my service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand your reaction very well. I just wanted to make sure that before, when he was making his request, he didn't give any specifics, as it were, of why he thought specifically Mr. Kvocka might be unreliable. I gather from what you say that he gave no such specifics. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that there were Serbs who were in cohorts with the Muslims. That is what he said. But he didn't say anything specific, to the effect that he had done this or that. His request boiled down to some sort of disobedience. I really don't know what he meant because I really didn't pay much attention, because that was not my line of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. The second part of the question, the last, is: When your anonymous friend told you later, just conversationally, that nothing had been done because Drljaca's requests were -- you used the word "too broad" and "technologically unfeasible." I understand about the technologically unfeasible part, you didn't have all the necessary technology to do, but when you say your understanding of what your -- the who person who communicated with you said as being too broad, did you take that to mean that Mr. Drljaca just wanted it on too many people or that his definition of the kinds of people that he wanted pursued in investigation was just plain too broad; in other words, his definition of "unreliability" was too all encompassing, took in too many people? Your understanding of what your associate who communicated this to you told you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that technical problems existed because there are certain pre-conditions. There mustn't be any obstacles in the way which further complicate the technology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that about "technological" and "feasible," but you would use the words "too broad" and "technologically unfeasible." I was interested in what you understood your associate to mean by "too broad."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what he meant was that too many people would require -- would be required for the job because there would have to be so many workers for collecting information. So if the number of people that Mr. Simo Drljaca wanted to be monitored, then we would have to have twice as many staff. So I think that is what he meant, plus the technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. I too have a couple of questions. You were working in the fifth department, which was also involved in defence preparations, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So one would say that there was a position in the police, the function being state security. So my question is: What exactly were your tasks in terms of information and defence preparations? What was your specific task?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My specific tasks were to train the members of the reserve force in various skills needed for the police. So as far as training is concerned, this covered 16 municipalities, and I was in charge of that. As I was trained in various disciplines, that was my task. Sometimes the chief of my department would join in and work with me, but I was mostly in charge of that, those activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that you were, in a sense, the teacher, the instructor?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You mentioned on a number of occasions that you had certain liaison tasks with the International Community, and in a response to Mr. Krstan Simic, you said this was because you spoke English that you were a liaison officer. What were your tasks specifically in connection the English language?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge of English is not fluent. I am just able to speak it and make myself understood, conveying meanings, simple meanings. I'm not able to correspond in English; I can just converse in English. So that my job was to grasp what it is they needed and to be able to take the necessary steps to meet their requests without needing an interpreter. They frequently had an interpreter with them, but there were occasions when a delegation would come without a proper interpreter. So the interpretation was mostly done by interpreters, and I was just there to arrange contacts and to make sure that those meetings took place without any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should it be understood that there were other liaison officers which dealt more with the substance, with the content? As you say, you were essentially a person for establishing contacts and bringing people together. Were there other people in charge of liaison in the substantive sense?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were not. I think that all liaison officers had the same status as I did, which means that they could arrange a contact and they would accompany the people to avoid any -- to make sure there were no incidents. But no one had the authority of an official organ to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. participate in the discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to go back to this story about your conversation with Simo Drljaca. You said that a certain Simo Miskic was also involved in this conversation. Was he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman, but he did not participate in the conversation. He was just mentioned. That is why I remember him, because I know him as a policeman. He used to come to Banja Luka. I saw him on a number of occasions, so I know him from that time period. I found it strange that he should be mentioned among the group of unreliables. I don't know exactly what it was he could have done, but I never conveyed that opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you knew this person Simo Miskic.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you knew that he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have already said that you didn't know Kvocka, but did you know whether he was a policeman or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know, because the gentleman mentioned a list of four or five names without saying what they were. He didn't even say that Simo Miskic was a policeman, but I just happen to know that he was a policeman. So one could assume that these were doubts as to the loyalty of members of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another point. You said that the name "Kvocka" reminded you of an animal and this helped you to remember the name. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the association that allowed you to say that this happened at the beginning of the month of June? How do you happen to remember that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a rather specific situation in my own home. I'd rather not mention any names, but I was coming there for private reasons. So whenever I had some free time, I would go to that cafe for personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You don't need to tell us. But what is the link between that conversation with Simo Drljaca and the other situation? What is the link between the two?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't quite understand what you mean by "pioneers," the link with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be a misunderstanding. You said that you remember this conversation, about the beginning of the month of June, because at the time you went there, as far as I understood, a pioneer establishment, for private reasons which you did not wish to enter into or explain.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went, for private reasons, to the sports centre because of some personal relations I had with certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm asking you what is the link between the two. You remember the name "Kvocka" because you associated it with an animal, the name of an animal, I think you said. I want to know why you are telling us that this happened in the month of June. How did you link the two events together?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The link is that I have certain associations linked to those dates and a certain person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another question. You spoke about the professionalism or, rather, non-professionalism of Simo Drljaca. You mentioned that he was wearing white Adidas sneakers - surely we're not advertising anything now - and also that he was drinking. How do you understand professionalism? How should he behave, in your opinion, as a professional?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that he had a tendency to drink. I didn't meet with him often to be able to say that. But I saw that there was alcohol on the table, which meant that people were drinking, and I joined in when I came. As for my understanding of professional behaviour or my personal view of it is that an executive must set an example to others. A superior must set an example to others, starting from his clothing, his behaviour, his respect for certain legal norms and standards. We had some very strange behaviour by certain people in those days, which was all the result of the complex situation we were in. One such example was the behaviour of Mr. Simo Drljaca, which I found strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I think you have just finished your testimony. We wish to thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you a safe return home. I will ask the usher to accompany you out now and thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now going to have a half-hour break. Excuse me. We have another witness, don't we? I think we have some small questions to deal with before the next witness, but we'll do that after the break. So a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Before we introduce the next witness, Mr. Krstan Simic, may we have the documents that you want to tender into evidence. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have already mentioned the documents. They have been assigned numbers. We tabled a sufficient number of copies, and we uphold the request. My assistant has just warned me that document D37/1 has not been admitted, and they are conclusions dated the 11th of May, 1992. The number is 11/12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking off the bat, by heart, but I seem to have the impression that the documents yesterday were 38 and 39. We gave the number D38 because number D37 had already been admitted. Madam Registrar, what happened to D37? Has it been admitted or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it has not, Your Honour. It needs to be. This is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, with respect to this document, that is to say, document D37/1, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the Chamber will allow me to just take a quick look at it and see if it's one of ours that's just been relabelled. It's already in evidence, Your Honour, as 2/4.22, put in through us. Mr. Saxon has assisted me in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the situation is rather complicated. What we can conclude is that the same document will have the number 2/4.22 and another number which is D37/1. Am I right in understanding that the same document has been assigned these two numbers, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we should do everything in our power to avoid one and the same document being assigned one, two, three, or four numbers, because otherwise we're going to have a mix-up. We could have a document with, let us suppose, six numbers because the Prosecution has one number for it and each of the Defence teams have the rest, five other numbers. So let us try to avoid that absurdity when designating numbers to documents. What I understand now is that Mr. Krstan Simic has no further documents to tender; is that correct?. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes. Just that one and the two documents mentioned yesterday, which were 38 and 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Ms. Susan Somers, I think that you have at least three documents, is that correct, to tender.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From today, yes, of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 2/2.7, 2/3.39, and 2/1.1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I indicate they are in already. They were admitted into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think there's a problem with the transcript there. We seem on it lagging behind, but we're catching up. We've caught up. Very well. So are those the documents that you see indicated on the screen? The only difference being is that the last document was the map, and it was document 2/1.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just -- that is correct. We just wanted to make sure that the Chamber was aware that these documents had been admitted into evidence in the document collection which preceded the composition of this Chamber with the other Chamber in 1999, and, therefore, some of these come before you now and perhaps you have not had a chance to look at them because they weren't pointed out specifically. If I may, just to try and assist the Chamber, our staff, if we have Friday, would like to meet with the Registry to try to go over some of these documents and where there is duplication, identify, for example, if Defence Exhibit D1.5 is the same as previously exhibited 2 point something. If we can work toward making, at least beginning some type of a chart or list, I think this would assist all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think we should look into the question, because the system that we were using was that the documents were presented by the parties with a number for identification, and here we decide whether the document is to be admitted or not. Now, what you are saying to me, I think, Ms. Somers, is that those documents have already been admitted into evidence, tendered. Were they admitted? Yes. So when we present documents in the courtroom, we must distinguish between whether they are new documents and need to be tendered or whether they have already been admitted and we're just making use of the documents. I think that would facilitate matters and we ought to pay attention to the question. As I say, if the documents have already been admitted, then we don't need to discuss the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we thank you for raising this. If we have in any manner contributed to the confusion, we apologise. I think we used the term "recall" to distinguish from new admission, but if not, we shall do that in the future and indicated clearly that these are admitted and that they're simply recalled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but let us pay attention to that. Otherwise, this can lead to confusion, although, confusions are very often useful because we have to clear them up if they exist, but not as the regular order of the day. So as I say, if the documents have already been admitted, then there's no point in discussing it further. Then let us take up our work where we left off, and we come to the introduction of the next witness. Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is some other point you wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we had asked the registrar if we could just inform the Chamber pursuant to yesterday's inquiry about the status of three matters before the witness comes in. One is the matter of the use of the psyche valuations for the accused Radic. The Chamber reinquired of us if we were willing to accept them or how we wished to proceed. I must inform the Chamber that because of the nature of this evidence, we would clearly need to cross-examine the psychologist or psychiatrist. Other types of expert reports perhaps on a case-by-case basis we might be able to arrive at a -- as I think the Chamber suggested, submitting our own response, a challenge plus our own response, but this type of evidence, in my opinion, is not susceptible of that type of action, so we ask the Chamber -- we simply inform the Chamber of our assessment of the situation. On the Kvocka exhibits, our staff checked, and we have no Defence Exhibit for accused Kvocka above number 55. The list that was submitted to us by Mr. Simic starts higher than that, and we have not had any of those exhibits handed to us for our assessment. As soon as that is done, we will very gladly report back to the Chamber and to counsel about acceptance or not or comments on. And the third matter. We were asked yesterday -- well, we were reminded that we owe a filing on the accused Zigic's motion for lifting the confidentiality, and we anticipate filing that this afternoon. I just wanted to let the Chamber know the status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Ms. Susan Somers. I don't know whether Mr. Krstan Simic wishes to inform us matters regarding documents above number 55, beyond number 55. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have disclosed -- we shall be presenting them to the opposite side. We thought that they were in agreement in view of the documents that they handed over to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This seems to be a game of ping-pong. Perhaps the Prosecutor has not received sufficient identification with respect to the documents that have been sent it, and maybe -- but perhaps you stem from the idea that the Prosecution already had the documents. Is that right, Mr. Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I will tender the documents tomorrow, and the problem will be solved as far as the Defence is concerned, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If there are no other outstanding matters, let us move on to the second witness called by the Kvocka Defence. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we call witness Jadranko Mikic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jadranko Mikic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now be reading the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming. You are going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Krstan Simic, your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Good morning to you for the second time, Mr. Mikic. As you know, my name is Krstan Simic, and together with Mr. Lukic, we represent the Defence team of Mr. Kvocka, and I shall be asking you a number of questions as the Defence team. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: For the record, could you give us your full name and surname, please?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: My name is Jadranko Mikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
