utterances.text: On the 17th of June, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, where I reside at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you employed today?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: In the State Security Service of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, where did you get your education?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: The Internal Affairs School in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Before that, primary school?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I graduated from primary school in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How long did your education in the Internal Affairs School last?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Four years. There were two generations per three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you remember when you enrolled for your first year of studies and when you completed your studies?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: In 1973 was when I enrolled and I graduated in 1976, in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What kind of school was it? Can you describe it to us?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: It is a specialised school of a boarding school type where cadres are trained for police business for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was that the only school of that type in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did members of other ethnic groups, other nationalities, living in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time attend that school?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Enrolment was done according to the parity system, which means that members of all the nationalities were enrolled depending on the population percentages. Now, what per cent to which nation, I can't tell you exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the spirit nurtured in the school through tuition, through training, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: At that time it was the spirit of brotherhood and unity; that is to say, the members of all the ethnic groups were trained and educated together and it was on the basis of brotherhood and unity for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: At the school, were there any divisions amongst the pupils?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. That was something that could not even have been conceived of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: From the regions we come from, did some people go to school with you?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, Milan Gavrilovic from Prijedor, Alija Pehadzic, Miroslav Kvocka. Those are some of them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you use the term we use, klasic, when speaking about the pupils in the school?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This referred to the members of one year, one class of education, one generation. We were the fourth generation and we would refer to each other as people of the same class, or "klasic" in our language.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was your training programme like?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: We could divide our training programme into three stages, approximately. One of those would be general subjects taught in other secondary schools; the second would be professional subjects which the police need to know; and thirdly, training in the martial arts, the use of weaponry, military doctrine, and similar subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, let us speak in more specific terms. The school in Sarajevo that you went to, was it a school belonging to the MUP, a part of the MUP only for the uniformed militia, as we referred to it at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you receive marks/assessments at the school?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said that you met Mr. Kvocka at the school.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you friends with him? Did you become close?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because we were from neighbouring towns, and we were perhaps more friendly than the others because we had more points in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka complete the school, graduate from it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of pupil he was; good or bad?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka was among the top ten pupils on the basis of his marks and his conduct, and as a reward for that, he had the right to choose his employment after graduation.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned conduct/behaviour. What does that imply?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Well, the teachers fill out a personal dossier for a pupil's conduct and behaviour and his development during his years of education, his marks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did the teachers look at the pupil's relationship with his fellow students?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the number one point to which attention focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that as one of the best pupils of that fourth generation at the school, he had the right to choose his place of employment. Do you know whether he made use of that opportunity?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He chose Prijedor because that is his native town.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You have already answered this next question of mine indirectly but give me a direct answer, please. In the four years of education and training at the school, and the time you spent together in the boarding school, did you ever notice on the part of Mr. Kvocka any negative nationalistic feelings towards the members of other ethnic groups or anything of that kind, any burgeoning of a feeling of that kind?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, for the precise reasons that I mentioned a moment ago. That was out of the question. Nobody could conceive of such things. On the other hand, as far as I was able to notice, his best friend was Alija Pehadzic from Prijedor. At that time I did not attach any great significance to that. I just knew they were friends, colleagues, that they'd grown up together and that that's why they were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After you had completed your schooling at this same school, did you ever meet Mr. Kvocka again?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where, when, and how?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: We met in the police station of Prijedor because I went to work there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How long did you work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I worked there between 1976 up until the beginning of 1979. Afterwards I transferred to Omarska for another year.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You didn't have an apartment in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, because I am from Banja Luka and I had no family in Prijedor. So I was accommodated in the apartment of the family of Alija Pehadzic. There was his mother and his two sisters; the father had been killed in a traffic accident. I lived there for one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Is that the same Mr. Alija Pehadzic who went to school with you [Realtime transcript read in error "for one year"] and Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When he returned to Prijedor, did Mr. Kvocka continue to have friends amongst the Muslim and Croat policemen? Was there any intimation of any nationalistic feelings?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have an objection to the transcript. It was stated that Mr. Pehadzic went to school just for one year. Let me ask the question again to put that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Pehadzic go to the first form with you and did all four years of the schooling?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he attended the school for all four years and received an award for the best marksman in the school. So he attended for four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you left Omarska, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: The Public Security Station of Banja Luka, that is to say, the police station which was referred to as Centre 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, I see that there are two people in the transcript. Perhaps it's the same person. Perhaps we could have the name spelt out. There is a Mr. Pehadzic and a Mr. Pejasic, so perhaps we could have the name spelled out. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The individual that we spoke about, could you tell us his name slowly?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Alija Pehadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So that means we're talking about Alija Pehadzic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, during 1991, have there been any disturbances in that area?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: In 1991, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a military conflict broke out, and the circumstances are widely known.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know that at one moment there occurred a division, that the Serbian part of the police separated from the rest of the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Actually, a lot about it was written in the media but we didn't get involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the police, were you or anyone else addressed by the head of the CSB, the commander of the public security station, asking you, "Gentlemen/Comrades, are you in favour of a part of the police force controlling the Serbian territories separating from the rest of the police force?"

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did you -- when you learnt this news, did anything change in the method of work of the police, in their application of the regulations?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Basically no.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you receive any new instructions such as, "From this day onwards you shall work in this way"?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. Everything remained approximately as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You've been a policeman for a long time. What do the uniformed part of the police act upon?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: The orders of their superior, pursuant, of course, to the law on internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In that year, 1992, was the law on internal affairs changed?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: The law on internal affairs was adopted by a decision of the Minister. I believe it was in 1975. A year or two later - I think in 1977 - it was officially enacted on the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That law is still in force with very minor changes. The substance of the law is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you speaking about the law or the rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the law on internal affairs, that is, the rules of our service.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you familiar with those rules of service?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do these rules of service regulate the obligations and procedures?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, very specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, you said that both in Prijedor and in Omarska and also in Banja Luka, you worked at the police station. Can you tell us, please, at the police station, what persons are in superior positions?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: That is the commander of the station, the deputy commander of the station, and two or more assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, what does the number of those assistants depend on?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: It depends on the size of the station and the territory it covers.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The police station called Centre 1 is a large one. Did it have a lower form of organisation, a branch?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: It had a commander, a deputy commander, assistants, assistant commander for crime, and assistant commander for traffic control.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I don't believe you quite understood me. I was not talking about the command structure. I was talking about a sub-unit maybe.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Like all stations, it had services, the beat service, the patrol service, it had outposts. Those would be the sections of the police station. Specifically, those outposts were in Vrbas and in Bronzani Majdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you mentioned these outposts in Bronzani Majdan and in Vrbas, were they in separate buildings from the police station?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So they had their own buildings?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were they integral parts of the basic police station?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The commander of the basic police station, was he also in command of the policemen in, say, Bronzani Majdan?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did this section have a commander, a superior officer, and what was his name?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: It had its section commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did the station commander -- was the station commander also his commander as well as the commander of other policemen?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are there deputy commanders in the section or assistants?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So the line of command ends with the commander of the outpost or section and starts with the station commander?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It ends and begins with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned that you worked in Prijedor and your activity was linked to the activity of the CSB. In the police station of Prijedor of the police - I'm not talking about the traffic police - were there any subsections?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: There were three of them, three sections, Ljubija, Kozarac, and Omarska. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to present a document to this witness, that is, communication sent by Simo Drljaca to the Security Services Centre Banja Luka. It is numbered 11/12/20-31 of the 29th of May, 1992. I would like this to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a new document, Mr. Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes. This document has never been used before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because when we're talking about a new document, we need help to have it distributed. When we are just recalling a document, we don't distribute it. So what will be the number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may continue, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, you have in front of you a dispatch. Is that a normal way of communication between lower instances towards superior ones?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the corner above it says "DX." What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: It's not encoded dispatch. It's a normal dispatch going through regular channels to subordinates and superiors. In this case, the chief, Simo Drljaca, is informing the CSB of Banja Luka and the head of the centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Please tell me, this paragraph 1 I will quote, it says: "In Prijedor there is one police station with general authority, with three branch stations (Omarska, Kozarac, and Ljubija) police departments." Are these the departments or sections you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are the ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, we mentioned this -- the turmoil we have all lived through, and I would like to ask you a question. Where does your wife come from?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: From Piskavica. That is a small village on the border of Omarska. It belongs to the Banja Luka municipality, whereas Omarska is part of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the police circles, in the year 1992, did you have any opportunity to hear any rumours about Mr. Kvocka, and if so, what were those rumours?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were triggered by an incident which I can mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: It was in the first half of 1992, in the CSB of Banja Luka. The story circulated that an anonymous report or denunciation came concerning mister -- addressed to Drljaca. It was also being said that the author was Miroslav Kvocka. All this was connected with the fact that Miroslav Kvocka was married to a Muslim, that his sisters had married Muslims, and the entire context concerned this fact. It said that he is not a person to be trusted, that he had links with Muslims, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was your reaction to those rumours, if I can call them that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't like it, honestly, in view of the time, the years we had spent together, because I knew the kind of man he was and his character, his integrity. I couldn't believe those stories. So I availed myself of one opportunity when I was in Piskavica with my wife, visiting her parents, to go and visit Miroslav and to tell him of those rumours and to warn him as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Warn him against what in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Well, since it was the year 1992, at the time of the armed conflict, very unstable times when anything could happen, things were going out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, you are a policeman. You have lived through all that happened there. Was there a real danger for someone who was labelled by anyone as a collaborator with the enemy nation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, I must warn you that you are asking the witness for an opinion. So you mustn't object later on. I'm just warning you. Do you understand what I've just said? You're asking the witness to express an opinion. Just so that it be known. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it dangerous in these times to be labelled as a collaborate with the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was more than dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Now did Mr. Kvocka react to what you told him, to this warning about the rumours?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: He simply couldn't believe it. Because we had known each other for a long time, we talked very sincerely. I conveyed to him all that I had heard, and I told him my personal opinion that this could be very dangerous. And it really could. There were many drunken fools, there are many paramilitary formations around, and anything could have happened. Things could have run out of control regardless of who you were and what you were doing. However, Miroslav said that he was trying to do his job as he was trained to do it, as we were taught, and he thought that all of that would simply pass, go away.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you were doing your duties as a policeman, were you ever on the beat?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What were you, exactly, in that system?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have any particular position?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I was a beat officer, a street-duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you ever on patrol?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I was an escort, a partner to a patrol officer, the leader of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What does that mean, an escort to the leader of the patrol sector?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: As a rule, it's a young policeman, a junior policeman, or a policeman who comes from a different area, not a local man.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The patrol sector leader or patrol area leader, what were his duties?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: This leader could be a senior policeman in terms of years of service, but not necessarily. But of primary importance is that he is a local man because he knows the people who live there and he knows the territory, the layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Why is it important for him to know the terrain and the people?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Because it facilitates contacts with people; it enables him to do his job, to fulfil the orders. If he knows the people in the field, that facilitates his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the difference between the escort and the patrol sector leader?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Basically, there was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In conclusion, you have just said you now work in the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And you graduated from the school for uniformed police staff. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber when and how you came to work in this service?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I'll come back to a detail I mentioned earlier to make things clearer. In 1994, I transferred to the Crime Investigation Service. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. continued to work in the police station Centre 1 but in mufti. That was perhaps a promotion as a reward for my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you become a superior officer or did you receive a higher rank?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. The rank is the same. I just stopped wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: In 1996, I was transferred to the entourage of the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajko Kasagic. I was his escort ex officio. Automatically, I transferred to the State Security Service because the Public Security Service does not provide escorts to the Prime Minister; that's not their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So since 1995 you have been in the State Security Sector of the CSB of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. There appear to be other Defence counsel that have a comment to make. Mr. Nikolic, no? Mr. Stojanovic, no? Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned the leader of the patrol sector and his escort. Is there a lower level than this escort of the leader of the patrol sector among regular police officers?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who gives orders to whom, the leader of the patrol sector to the escort or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Actually, the leader of the sector should be in command. He is usually a more experienced policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So let us repeat: This escort of his has absolutely no command authority over the leader of the patrol service.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Jovan Simic, no questions? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers? I see it's Mr. Waidyaratne for the cross-examination. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said many things about Mr. Kvocka. Could you tell us whether you knew him before you came to Sarajevo, to the School of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you explain -- the three years that you spent in the school and subsequently, you said that you were good friends or more friendly. Could you explain as to what this association was?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: As we were young in those days, actually children, we were far from home, we were in a boarding school, and naturally we tended to become close, especially people coming from the same environment, the same village, the same town. So we had much more in common and it was quite normal for us to become close. That is how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That's during the school days, the association of friendship that you had with him.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After that, when you resumed police duties in the Prijedor Police Station, did you have the same relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I think we became even closer, because when you're working in the police, your colleague, your partner, whatever you like to call him, is a very important person in your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you discuss anything personal with him or, say, did you discuss any politics with him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What were the personal matters that you discussed with him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Many things. In those days, we were young. We would talk about girlfriends, outings, a little about work, the usual topics that interested us in those days. Nothing of special importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you discuss anything about his family, how many family members he had, or what his father was doing about the financial difficulties that he had?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. In those days, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know how many brothers he had?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Have you ever asked him about his family members?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Rarely. As I have already said, when I graduated from school, I was 18 and those were not subjects that interested us at that age.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka, at any time, discuss with you politics or any political convictions or commitments he had?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, no. As far as I'm aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You don't know what he was or what his political commitments or convictions were.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, he was a policeman, first and foremost. And in those days when we were being educated, there was no politics for us. Absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: While you were working in the Prijedor Police Station, did you know any other -- did you know a person by the name of Radic, Mladen Radic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I know the name but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During your entire life in the police - even still you're a police officer - you have not come across the name of -- the person by the name of Mladen Radic, Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I have heard the name but I don't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, I will come to things that you've said about you. After you left Omarska -- the Prijedor Police Station, sorry, the Prijedor Police Station, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I worked in the Banja Luka CSB, the centre police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During the 1992 conflict, if I may be specific, during the month of May and in August 1992, where were you working?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: The police station called Centre 1, motorised patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you tell us which areas you overlooked?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Centre 1 covers the downtown area as the name implies. It is a large part of downtown Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During this time, were you assigned any special assignments?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, no. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know during this time that there were many non-Serbs - Muslims, Croats - that went in convoys, a convoy towards Karlovac, through the mountains of Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I was aware of that report. I had heard that that was going on. But as for the routes, I cannot confirm that. But my answer to the first part of your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What did you hear about?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I heard that citizens of non-Serb ethnicity were leaving Banja Luka out of fear from the war, out of fear for their own personal safety probably, and I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you hear that people who were detained in the camps, like Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, were in these convoys?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was police escort provided to these convoys?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I could not guarantee it, but probably there was a police escort or a military escort. That is what should have happened, according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were you aware that such escort was provided?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you in any of these escorts.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know that many -- during the month of August, on the 21st of August, 1992, around 250 non-Serbs were killed at the Vlasic Mountain when they were going in a convoy to Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: That there were many rumours and stories about all sides, but these specific facts that you are mentioning is that I could not confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And about these rumours and stories that you heard, did you hear that these convoys were under police escort?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: People were going away. These were horrible times. People were leaving en masse and others were coming too from all over. Some people were going in one direction; others were coming in another. There was no full control over these movements. It was just not possible. Everything was based on rumours and hearsay, as people would say, but no very specific data could be obtained probably on any of the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The people who were leaving, the non-Serbs who were leaving the Prijedor area and the Banja Luka area, were they -- did they have free movement or were they escorted out or forced out?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, they had freedom of movement, that's for sure. People could come and go as they wished. As for organised departures and arrivals, there were those as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, were there roadblocks, checkpoints during this time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And were these people -- the people at the checkpoints, did they check the movements of the others who moved around? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Checkpoints are put up in specific locations in towns and villages, and the army or the police, depending on the orders and who mans the checkpoint, they check movement of persons, vehicles, goods through those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, just one more question. Now, the rumour that you -- the rumours and the stories that you heard, especially the incident that I referred to on the 21st of August, 1992, the killing of around 200 to 250 non-Serbs at the Vlasic Mountain, was it a rumour or that you heard in your official capacity?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I told you that I had not heard this news report personally. I am not familiar with that report. I absolutely don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Have you ever visited the two camps, Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You are aware that certain people were released from those camps?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything specific about that as I had no contact with those camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I refer to the document just produced by the Defence marked as D40/1. Can that be given to the Witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to read that document, Mr. Mikic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: This is a document which is supposed to have been signed by Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Dated 28th May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you were referred by the learned counsel, were you, for Mr. Kvocka, to the first paragraph. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please read out the second paragraph? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need to make the witness read it. Just put your question to the witness. I'm sorry, Mr. Krstan Simic. We're going to speed things up, so please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 says: "Before the conflict broke out, there were 107 active policemen, 26 of them from the Kozarac area. A number of these policemen were killed in combat operations and the others are in the collection centre." Am I correct? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, what is your objection? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a dispatch sent by the head of the public security station to the head of the centre of the security services, and I really don't see what point there is asking Mr. Mikic to comment on this report when he is an escort, the escort of the leader of the patrol sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I think there's no problem in putting this question to the witness. If the witness knows something, he will tell us. If he doesn't, he will say no. We're wasting a lot of time with these interruptions and questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is it stated in the document?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mikic, you must be quite familiar with the area of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You have not been to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I have. I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know that there is a police station in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know as to any of these people who served in Kozarac, the policemen?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I knew them by sight. I think Dedukic was the station commander, something like that. Then a colleague of mine called Milos worked there, and I think Ibrahim Denic worked there for a time and then he was transferred to Omarska. As far as I can remember, those are the people I can think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sure as an experienced police officer, you must know that Kozarac was predominantly a Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know as to what happened to the police officers of Muslim ethnicity after the takeover in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. There was an armed conflict, many policemen were killed, many were wounded, and any further details, I don't know. In those days it was impossible to keep track of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you sign a loyalty oath, a Serb loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mikic, I will come to the meeting that you had with Mr. Kvocka. Could you tell us roughly when you had this meeting with Mr. Kvocka at the Omarska centre?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in June. I think the first half of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: According to Mr. Kvocka's testimony, it is almost after a year that you have met him in Omarska in 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It was after a long time. During this time of the ethnic conflict, if I may narrow down the period, 1992, April and in August, how many times did you meet Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I think only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And is it correct that it was the time that you met him at the Omarska centre?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Had you had time -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness never said he met Mr. Kvocka in the Omarska centre, because from that one could conclude that they went to the centre to have that meeting, the camp. They actually met in the village of Omarska, in the centre of the village of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: If I may answer this question, Your Honour. I'm referring to the testimony given by Mr. Kvocka on the 2nd of March, 2000. According to Mr. Kvocka, he said he met Mr. Mikic at the Omarska centre and, in fact, he had gone for coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question to the witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, but in the centre of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question to the witness, Mr. Waidyaratne, and then we'll review all that. Give the Chamber a little leeway and we will clarify these things. So put your question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you meet Mr. Kvocka in the month of June?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: To make things quite clear, Omarska is a small locality which has two main streets, and everything that happens there usually happens in the centre of that village. That is where there is a general store, two or three cafes. So everything centres around those two streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have coffee with Mr. Kvocka on that day? Surely you must remember that.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you discuss anything personal, other than the discussion that you testified to today?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you tell us as to what it was?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: We discussed what the two of us were doing, what he was doing, what I was doing, whether we were having any difficulties. That was the subject of greatest interest to us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka say what he was doing at that time? Did he say that he was attached to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What else did he say?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: He told me that temporarily he was working in the investigations centre - that is how he described it - the investigations centre of Omarska and that there were very many problems because everything was pure improvisation. Nothing had been put in order; nothing was working as it should.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He said temporarily, or is it that you got the indication that it was temporary?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: That was not my impression. It has to be temporary because these were extraordinary circumstances. He couldn't have been working there on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a permanent basis; it was quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did he say as to what functions he had to perform in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, no. He said that he was on duty there, that he had a table, and he said, "I've got a telephone for contacts." That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What are the difficulties that he spoke about?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: He spoke about the problems. To make things clearer for you, we are trained policemen. We're used to order and discipline so that everything should be according to procedure. If that is lacking, we have a problem, which means that we are not able to perform our duties in the way we should.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka speak about his former colleagues being detained at the centre -- at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. But he said that his commander, Zeljo - Zelja, I think that's how he called him, I don't know him personally - was endeavouring to improve things but that he was having very little success.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka speak about Fikret Harambasic, Avdagic --

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: -- that these people were detained at the camp and they were detained in subhuman conditions?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He never said anything about non-Serbs, his former colleagues, who were detained at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: By name, we did not discuss anyone in person. But he told me that the situation was bad and that the persons coming there were not in a good condition. Because that was an investigations centre, that is how it was called in those days, it was not a camp at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that the conditions were bad. What did he say about the conditions? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Well, that the food was poor, the accommodation was poor; that they were not able to provide proper food or proper accommodation. They lacked the facilities to provide relatively normal conditions for the time we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did he speak about his brothers-in-law?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, the witness already told you that they spoke in general terms, without mentioning names. If we are going to ask about names, then the witness will tell you that they didn't talk about that person. He told you that they spoke in general terms. So please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kvocka say that he took certain family members to the investigative centre and later on took them back home?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. It's the first time I'm hearing of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When Mr. Kvocka spoke about the conditions in the camp, did he say that he was trying to improve the conditions in the camp? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question was put to the witness and the witness explicitly said that his commander, Zeljo, was endeavouring to improve things. In answer to the question as to what Kvocka was doing there, the witness answered that he was on duty there. So I don't know what the purpose of this question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, it's an important question. So put your question to the witness, Mr. Waidyaratne, in a very concrete form.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, when he spoke about the conditions in the camp, did he say that he was trying to improve the conditions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. I've already told you, he was mentioning his commander Zeljo - I personally don't know this man, Zeljo - and that he was endeavouring with superiors in Prijedor to improve conditions, to do something - to improve something, that's what he said - but that he was having little success, that he was not managing to achieve that properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, when you spoke about the rumours or the stories that you heard about Kvocka, the bad stories, you said that Mr. Kvocka was surprised. What else was -- what was his reaction thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how I could explain it to you. His reaction was that he had nothing against anyone. He went back to the period when we were undergoing training and when we were friends and the way we were taught. So his logic was, "If I have nothing against anyone or don't wish to do any harm to anyone," then surely he should not expect anyone else to harm him. Simply, I think he wasn't aware of the situation and the times we were in, or he became aware very, very late.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did he say that he was not engaging in any help to the people who were there in the camp, or that the rumours were incorrect, not true?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, no. As far as individuals or persons who were there, this was something we did not discuss, it's something I did not show any interest in. The reason for our meeting was upon my initiative because I wanted to convey to him what I had heard, so that this meeting didn't take long. We didn't discuss the people who were there; we never spoke about that by name or in any other way. That simply was not one of the topics of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry for interrupting you. How long did this meeting last?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't be precise about that now, but 30 to 40 minutes, on the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. How much more time do you need, Mr. Waidyaratne?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: A little more time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Can we have the adjournment now, Your Honour, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hoping we could finish with this witness before the break. I think your time has expired by now. In any event, we are unable to finish now so we'll have the lunch break. I was trying to release the witness but we'll see. So we'll have a 50-minute lunch break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the witness to leave before us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, as I said, a 50-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mikic, you can sit down. Are you now more comfortable after lunch? Very well. Thank you. So we are going to try and finish. Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'll be very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, you said that you heard rumours and stories about Mr. Kvocka when you were in Banja Luka. Did you take any action or do anything to clear up these rumours or stories about your friend Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: When I heard them, there was nothing much I could do about it. It was not in my competence. I am a policeman, as we say in our jargon, an infantryman. I have no authority. I don't have the power to do anything about it. The only thing I could do, I did, meet him, convey these things to him and warn him in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After the meeting that you discussed these rumours with Mr. Kvocka, when did you meet Mr. Kvocka after that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I don't think I did see him after that, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know that he was a policeman attached to the Prijedor opstina until his arrest?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was demoted or reprimanded or any action taken against him with regard to these rumours or the suspicion that they had with regard to him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: All I can give you is my personal opinion, if it means anything to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, in your direct examination, you spoke of turmoil in the area. What turmoil existed for the Serbians since they were in control of the territory? The Chamber has heard much evidence that after the takeover, without a single bullet being fired, and that many non-Serbs were taken to the camps and they were detain. What -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The witness was speaking about the situation in Banja Luka. He doesn't live in Prijedor, and he wasn't speaking of events in Prijedor or the establishment of camps and the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Simic answered the question now. If the witness was referring to Banja Luka, he could have said that. But I thought it was in general that he was talking about, the general situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the purpose of this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: To show that there was no such turmoil or any difficulties that these people faced during that time, as they were in control of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, perhaps you should rephrase the question, because you have just stated an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, did you have any difficulties or have any bad periods during the takeover, or during the conflict that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I did, just as anyone else. Regardless of ethnicity, we had the same problems; lack of food, water, electricity, all the problems associated with such conflicts. It was the same for everyone. The police, under those circumstances, worked very hard, under very difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, other than being a policeman, were you not able to move freely during this time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Well, basically, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you not provided with food? Were you not -- didn't you have sufficient food?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, are there any additional questions? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, when you spoke about the police station, before these events and during those events and today, the police station, does it have any powers to conduct investigations regarding any criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: The police station, you mean uniformed policemen? No. There is a special service dealing with that; we call that the Criminal Investigation Service. The police only bring people into custody, make reports about certain information, and that's where their work ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As an institution of that kind, do you receive any reports saying, for instance, "Four murders were committed in Drakulic; five in Knezevo," or are these reports sent somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does the police station, I'm talking about part of the Security Services Centre, does it receive reports about grave criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: All of such reports come into the CSB and then they are forwarded to the relevant service, the Crime Investigation Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does the police station receive them?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does he inform the policemen under him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, do you have any additional questions? No. Well, then, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mikic.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'd like just to follow up some of your statements in case you can clarify it more. Concerning the denunciation which was made against Mr. Kvocka - you informed him about it and you explained it to him - did he, from your assessment, react to it? Did he try to counteract it by a certain action, by trying to prove that he was not a sympathiser, for instance, or even a collaborator of the Muslims? What would he do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. I said it once before, I believe that Mr. Kvocka was not quite aware of the times we were living in and he was not aware of what his environment was like. He simply couldn't understand it. His life creed was "I'm a good man and I expect everyone to be good to me." That is not the proper thinking for a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, what happened to other people who were sympathisers around you? Were they kicked out of their jobs? Were they in danger?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain this. It was not obvious, evident danger, life danger, but those people were under some sort of surveillance. It was a bit different. Because the very fact that Mr. Kvocka worked there as the duty officer in this investigations centre, he worked practically as a receptionist and it was a demotion for him as a policeman, because at school he was a good student, he was one of the best in Prijedor. On account of that, he even went to work in the security detail in one of our embassies; I don't know where it was, Vienna, Paris, somewhere. And the very fact that he was appointed to such a position after that was, in my view, a demotion, if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you considered that as the punishment for being a sympathiser?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was a punishment, but it was some form of degradation, demotion, rather, because he was working as a receptionist. It was not a real policeman's job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he was looked upon as not a very, let's say, aggressive policeman.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Mikic, you said that the rumour you heard about Mr. Kvocka in the spring of 1992 was that he was not to be trusted because he was, you used the word "connected," to Muslims. Was that rumour, as it reached your ears, based pretty much on the fact that he had relatives, his wife, his brothers-in-law, et cetera, who were Muslim, or did it go beyond that and the rumour was that he really believed in the same things they did, was sympathetic to them, would help them in their endeavours?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I think that was primarily due to his wife and his brothers-in-law, because his wife is a Muslim and his brothers-in-law, of course, as well. So I think that's where the -- from where the wind was blowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In that case, you said you felt it your duty as a friend to warn him. What could he be warned about if it was based upon the fact that it was his relatives? There wasn't anything he could do about that. Just to be aware of it or what?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Our friendship was a long-standing one. In the police, we all rely on each other. Our job is such that we always run risks. So there is a bond between us. I felt it was my duty to talk to him, to discuss it with him, to see what he has to say about it and whether he knew anything about it at all, whether he was aware of it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My second question is: When you did meet with him in June 1992 and he told you about his assignment to Omarska, to the camp, and I think you mentioned he said he had a table and a telephone, and you referred to him later on as basically a receptionist, did he, besides describing that part of his job, did he ever mention whether he had any title in the job, any official title in the Omarska camp, that he was a guard - I'm just using these as examples - a guard, a shift commander, a deputy commander, a commander, that he had any formal title? Did he ever mention if that was so?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No, not in that context, never. As for the table and the telephone set, he didn't tell me that. I heard someone saying something like, "They gave him a small table and a telephone set to play receptionist." That was said tongue-in-cheek. I don't even think it was a direct line with a connection to Banja Luka. It was just an intercom number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you say you heard that about the telephone and the table from somebody else. So while Mr. Kvocka was at the camp, there were still rumours circulating even in the period after you met with him in the Banja Luka office? People were still talking about him even after you had your conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Well, those were superficial gossip, superficial talk among people who knew each other. It was a narrow circle. As we would say, just mentioned in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is: After Mr. Kvocka left the camp and when he returned to other duties in the police system, did you hear any further rumours about him of any sort, after he left the Omarska camp and went back to other police duties, and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Nothing much. But he was no longer so popular in his locality, in his hometown, as he used to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you knew that he had left, or did you find out that he had left the camp at some point and was back in a different police job out in the community?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't really say yes or no, because I don't know. I don't know when it happened or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You mean you never heard anything during that summer about him as to whether or not he was still at the camp or he had left the camp and gone on to other duties?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. I had absolutely no further information about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And you didn't, I take it, make any inquiries as to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. just where he was, what he was doing, whether he was still at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't ask specifically about him. We usually ask about each other. I have friends, and when we meet, we discuss who is where and how the families are and whether a person is alive and well, and the rest is less important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And you did -- this is my last question. You said that you did hear at some time that when he went back to other police duties, he was less popular in his own community. When would you have heard that? Approximately what time would you have heard that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you. A lot of time has gone by, and I wouldn't like to say anything inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mikic, I have some very simple questions for you. Do you know Mr. Kvocka's wife?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And her sisters or brothers?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even today?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us a date as to when you heard these rumours, the rumours that we have discussed?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I'm really not able to do so, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you know when Mr. Kvocka left the Omarska centre?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I know that it was very shortly after our conversation. I think he stayed on after that for a very brief time, but I don't know the exact date. After that, I don't know where he went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So for a brief time after your conversation. So can you give us the date of your conversation then?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: I'm really not able to do that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you told us that this conversation lasted more or less half an hour. Do you remember where you met, the place or the coffee shop or where it was?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: It's not really a coffee shop. It's like a restaurant in the centre, at the crossroads of two roads in the very heart of Omarska. About 50 feet from the police station, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know Omarska well?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MIKIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Mikic. You have completed your testimony. We thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, do you wish to tender this document, D40/1? I think that's the only one. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Waidyaratne, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So document D40/1 is admitted into evidence. I believe, Mr. Krstan Simic, that you have a motion, a request. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have filed a motion for protective measures because obviously there was a misunderstanding at the Status Conference. I upheld my request and Ms. Somers did not oppose it. So we have just drafted it, and I made the submission through the registrar to you for protective measures for the following witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the following witnesses; is that right? For the next witness? For this next witness; is that right? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No. The witnesses which are due to come later, next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to call the next witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just let me hear the opinion of the Prosecutor because then we can proceed more quickly. Ms. Susan Somers, do you have any objection in relation to this motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the Chamber would grant me one moment to confer with my colleague, just to make sure I know exactly about whom this is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Krstan Simic said that he spoke to the Prosecutor, in accordance with our Rules, a motion first to be discussed by the other party and then filed. Is that correct, Mr. Krstan Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But there was a misunderstanding at the previous Status Conference at which Ms. Somers supported my request for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be a problem of translation because the translation was that Ms. Somers filed a motion. I think that's not right. What I gathered from the last Status Conference was that Ms. Somers would not have any objection on condition that -- but what I have in the transcript is: [In English] "... at the previous Status Conference at which Ms. Somers supported my request for protective measures." What is this, Madam Susan Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, without having the transcript in front of me, I doubt that I'd support it but I'd probably not object to it. And having reviewed the upcoming witnesses with my colleagues, we do not oppose these measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We're going to take advantage of the time. The Chamber is going to study your motion and make a decision. I thought it was for the next witness. But as it is for witnesses for next week, you will have a decision tomorrow or the next day. So the next witness now, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness is Lazo Basrak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May we clarify that? We had Mr. Basrak as the fifth witness, and if this is out of order, then I'm afraid we were given wrong information for our preparation. Mr. Basrak was listed as witness number 5, and we were told that this would be the absolute order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] It is correct that it is out of order, but we wanted to take advantage of the time, to use the little time we have left to hear this witness who is testifying only about two facts. He will be testifying very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, do you accept this change of order? I must remind you that the Prosecutor changed the order of their witnesses a great deal during your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly in principle, when a change comes up and it's completely unexpected. However, we only days ago established this order. These were witnesses who were added. We have had to scramble to put our basic cross together, and I would not be able to proceed at this time. We're blind-sided on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Why can't we just hear his direct? And then you've got overnight, if necessary, I mean if you feel you can't handle the cross, then you've got overnight. If it's that short, then you can surely put it together overnight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for offering that option. If we can, depending on the nature of it, if we determine that, we would still need an extra day because we had anticipated having it, I believe, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If it's very short and he gets through the direct today, or if he doesn't get through the direct today, you're an experienced lawyer, I know, in the courtroom, along with your colleagues, and I'm sure you could put together the cross overnight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We'll give it our very best effort. We only ask that if there are going to be these changes -- we've had multiple contacts and this was never raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We were just depriving Mr. Krstan Simic of his attempt to prove that he would begin and finish with this witness today; isn't that right, Mr. Krstan Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the Presiding Judge who is talking to you. You are going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Make yourself comfortable. Get closer to the microphone, please. First of all, let me say thank you for coming. For the moment, you are going to answer questions which will be put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic. After that, other counsel may have questions for you; then the Prosecutor and the Judges. Mr. Krstan Simic, your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Basrak.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: For the record, will you give us your exact name, please.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: My name is Lazar Basrak.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: On the 22nd of March, 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And where?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: In Niska Glava, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where are you residing now?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: Yes. Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is your status today? Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: I am a retired policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you working during your career in the police?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: I worked in Zagreb, the municipality of Velika Gorica.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: From when until when?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR BASRAK
utterances.text: From the 25th of October, 1976 until the 14th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was your wife working in Zagreb?
